units.text: The man outside the door has not, in the meantime, become a simple problem. We do not know all the causes of his situation. We do not know whether he will accept help, what kind of help he needs, or what can be achieved that evening. We have not discovered the biography that would give us the comforting feeling that he unquestionably deserves not to be abandoned.

We can begin with a respectful question and an assessment of the immediate need, without promising what we cannot do. We can seek appropriate support when the situation calls for it. We can avoid turning him into a spectacle. The next day, we can also ask why the only available solution was improvised by passersby. Immediate action and the institutional problem do not exclude each other.

Perhaps one of the people in the building indirectly caused some of the world's injustice. Perhaps another is barely staying on their feet. Perhaps someone helped yesterday and can do no more today. A responsible account does not assume it knows all this at a glance. Nor does it wait to know everything before making any possible gesture.

The child asks why the man is sleeping there. One easy answer would say that people end up where they deserve. Another easy answer would say that no one is responsible for anything, because everything has causes. Both would close the conversation too soon. A more honest answer would begin like this: we do not yet know all the reasons; some concern choices, others circumstances, and the fact that we do not know does not, by itself, tell us what to do now.

Perhaps responsibility is not a hidden property we find inside people, like eye color. Perhaps it is a practice through which we connect power to explanation, action to consequences, and vulnerability to justified demands. This practice can be unjust. It can be used to discipline the weak and protect the powerful. That is precisely why it must be examined, not abandoned.

The reality of suffering does not, by itself, settle every moral dispute. But it places a serious limit on the pleasure of treating everything as a game of concepts. Beyond our formulations, someone bears the consequences. A philosophy of responsibility is worth keeping insofar as it helps us see more precisely who bears them, who can bring about change, and what demand can be justified.

We will not leave this book with our innocence proven. Nor should we leave with the impression that we are personally obliged to repair the universe. Those would be two ways of avoiding the same work: identifying our share, examining it, and fairly distributing the rest.

That evening, someone opens the door. We do not know whether the gesture will solve much. We need not invent a happy ending to recognize its meaning. Sometimes responsibility begins precisely with refusing to demand certainty of a good ending before doing something justified.
